name: Thymulin

lead: Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the thymus that needs zinc to be active. It appears in peptide and zinc discussions as an immune and general-health option, not as a cosmetic one.

The chain runs from a zinc-dependent thymic hormone to immune regulation to general health. It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 and has been studied for T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation. Human data cover zinc status and thymic function, not supplement use.

paras: Some vendors sell it as a research peptide in longevity circles; users often pair the idea with attention to zinc intake.
No human safety trials of the peptide were found. It is not an approved drug and is sold unregulated.

angle.text: Thymulin is a thymus hormone that needs zinc to be active, discussed in peptide and zinc circles for immune and general health. Human data covers zinc status and thymic function; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Thymulin, also called facteur thymique sérique (FTS) or serum thymic factor, is a nine-amino-acid peptide (pGlu-Ala-Lys-Ser-Gln-Gly-Gly-Ser-Asn) produced by epithelial cells of the thymus and requiring zinc for biological activity [1][1]. Bach and colleagues described it in 1977 [1].

In the appearance context, thymulin is discussed in peptide and longevity-minded circles as part of a healthy-ageing and recovery idea: the thymus shrinks with age, thymulin levels fall, and low-grade inflammation rises, a pattern researchers call inflammaging [1][2]. People interested in ageing well, and in looking and feeling younger, sometimes include thymic peptides in that conversation. The link to how someone looks is therefore indirect and claimed, through immune and anti-inflammatory support rather than any direct effect on skin, hair or physique.

Research has concerned its role in T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation [1][2][3]. Laboratory and animal work is extensive, and human data are mostly measurements of circulating thymulin in relation to zinc status and nutrition. No human trials of thymulin as a treatment were found. It is sold by some vendors as a research peptide and is not an approved drug.

paras: Thymulin is a nonapeptide that begins with pyroglutamate and ends with asparagine. It carries a zinc ion, and its biological activity and antigenicity depend on that metal; without zinc the peptide is inactive [1][4]. A 1982 PNAS study showed that zinc and other metals contribute to the activity of serum thymic factor [5].

Thymulin is thought to help T-cell differentiation and to enhance T-cell and natural killer cell activity, acting largely locally on the thymus-dependent immune system [1]. An early review described it as a zinc-dependent hormone that induces T-cell differentiation and most notably affects suppressor T-cells, and anticipated clinical use as an immunoregulatory agent [4]. Reviews of thymic endocrinology describe how the thymus shrinks early in life, a process some authors call thymic menopause, and how thymic hormones, growth hormone, prolactin, melatonin and zinc have been used to try to counter thymic involution in animals [6][7].

Its secretion follows a circadian rhythm and is tied to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis: it interacts with that axis in both directions, and plasma levels correlate with ACTH [1][2][3]. A study in rats and humans reported that melatonin is responsible for the night-time rise of serum and thymic thymulin and thymosin alpha-1 [8]. A 1997 study found thymulin stimulated corticotropin release from rat anterior pituitary [1].

Recent research has focused on thymulin as a regulator of pro-inflammatory mediators. It appears to dampen activation of myeloid cells and cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha in part by inhibiting NF-kB signalling, while levels of those cytokines rise with age in rodents and humans and thymulin falls [1]. Wikipedia reports a 2026 Nature Communications study indicating that thymulin restrained age-associated myeloid inflammation and enhanced cancer immunotherapy in experimental models [1].

Most human data connect thymulin to zinc. A 1988 study found serum thymulin activity fell in mildly zinc-deficient volunteers and recovered after zinc supplementation [9]. Trials in other groups measured thymulin after zinc supplementation, including patients with Crohn's disease, where zinc restored plasma zinc and thymulin [10], children with Down syndrome [11] and Gambian children [12]. A Nepalese study used thymulin concentration as a proxy for thymic size and function in adolescents whose mothers were in a vitamin A or beta-carotene supplementation trial [13].
A 2020 review proposed that precursors of thymic peptides in cell nuclei act as stress sensors that send distress signals to the immune system when cleaved [14].

A peptide analog of thymulin, called PAT, showed analgesic effects in animal studies and has anti-inflammatory neuroprotective effects in the central nervous system, where astrocytes appear to be the target [1]. Researchers hope thymulin analogs could eventually yield drugs against inflammation in neurodegenerative disease and rheumatism; this remains a research hope rather than an established therapy [1]. Reviews of thymic hormones in cancer note the evidence on thymic function and treatment response is still limited [15]. Wikipedia also notes an association between significantly lower thymulin levels and anorexia nervosa [1].

No studies found of thymulin as a treatment. The human data that exist concern zinc status and circulating thymulin activity [9][10][11][12], and thymulin concentration as a marker of thymic function in nutrition studies [13]. An analog peptide has been examined in animal models of pain and neuroinflammation [1].

Thymulin is offered by some vendors as a research peptide and is not an approved drug. Its presence in looksmaxxing and longevity discussion is minor: the clearest community mentions are older T Nation posts that describe arginine as raising blood levels of thymulin as evidence that it restores thymic endocrine function [16][17]. No appearance outcomes have been studied.
